procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 17, 1962 of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in Misc. Appeal No. 22 of 1962.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No. 1 filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High Court took the view that the present appellant could have no interest in the properties left by Jangi Jogi. It reversed the District Judge's decision.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, in forma pauperis (as a poor person), appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave because the High Court dismissed her suit for a declaration of ownership and possession of the suit properties.

directions: The decision of the High Court has to be reversed and that of the District Judge restored.
The appeal is thus allowed with costs here and in the High Court.
The amount of court fee shall be recovered by the Government from respondent No. 1 in accordance with Order 17, Rule 8 of the Supreme Court Rules.
Costs of appellant's Advocate to be taxed against Respondent No. I and made recoverable from him.

issue.issue_text: Whether a co-plaintiff could transfer all her rights to the defendant, who was a trespasser, by merely filing a petition stating she did not wish to prosecute the suit.

facts: An appellant and a co-plaintiff (Jugli Bai) sued a defendant for possession of properties.
The trial court found that the defendant was a 'mere trespasser' and that the appellant had been in possession until dispossessed by him.
During the suit, the co-plaintiff (Jugli Bai), who was considered a rightful heir, entered into a compromise with the defendant.
The co-plaintiff filed a petition stating she did not wish to prosecute the suit and was withdrawing her claim.
law: A person in possession of property has a 'possessory title' which is sufficient evidence of ownership against a person who has no title and is a mere wrong-doer or trespasser.
A transfer of property rights cannot be legally effected by one party merely filing a petition to withdraw from a lawsuit in favor of another party.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the High Court's decision, which had held that the defendant was 'clothed with the very same rights' as the co-plaintiff because of the compromise and withdrawal.
The Supreme Court found this reasoning to be an error and 'somewhat difficult to understand'.

The Court reasoned that if the defendant was a mere trespasser, as the trial court found, it was impossible for the co-plaintiff to transfer all her property rights to him simply by filing a petition to withdraw from the suit.
The Court emphasized that such a petition is not a valid method for transferring legal rights to property.

Furthermore, the Court noted that the appellant had her own possessory title, which entitled her to seek restoration of possession from a trespasser, and this right was not defeated by the compromise between the co-plaintiff and the defendant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view, holding that a co-plaintiff could not transfer her property rights to a defendant, who was a trespasser, simply by filing a petition stating she no longer wished to prosecute the suit. This act was not a valid means of effecting a transfer of rights.

issue.issue_text: Whether a plaintiff's possessory title is sufficient evidence of title to obtain restoration of possession against a defendant who is a mere trespasser with no title.

facts: The appellant (plaintiff) was in possession of certain properties.
The trial court found that the respondent was a "mere trespasser" and had illegally occupied the properties.

The High Court dismissed the appellant's suit, reasoning that another person, Jugli Bai, was the rightful heir and had entered into a compromise with the respondent, thereby "clothing" the respondent with her rights.
law: The Court established the principle that a plaintiff's possession is sufficient evidence of title as owner when asserted against a defendant who has no title.

The Court referenced Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act (1877), which allows a person dispossessed without due process to recover possession within six months, even against someone who might have a better title.

Reasoning from this, the Court argued that if a plaintiff can recover possession from someone who might have a title, it is "certainly right and just" that they should be able to recover possession from a defendant who is a "mere wrong-doer" with no title at all.
application: The Supreme Court applied the principle that possessory title is sufficient against a trespasser to the facts of the case.
It held that the High Court was in error for dismissing the appellant's suit based on the compromise between Jugli Bai and the respondent.

The Court reasoned that if the respondent was indeed a mere trespasser, as the trial court found, then a compromise with a third party (Jugli Bai) could not retroactively grant him rights to defeat the appellant's claim, which was based on her prior possession.
Therefore, the appellant's possessory title entitled her to have her possession restored because the respondent had no right, title, or interest in the property.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a plaintiff's possessory title is sufficient evidence of title to obtain restoration of possession against a defendant who is a mere trespasser with no title of their own.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the appellant's suit on the ground that a co-plaintiff had entered into a compromise with the defendant.

facts: The appellant and a co-plaintiff (Jugli Bai) sued the defendant (respondent No. 1) for possession of properties.
The trial court found that the appellant had been in possession until she was dispossessed by the defendant, who was found to be a mere trespasser.
During the suit, the co-plaintiff, Jugli Bai, entered into a compromise with the defendant and withdrew her claim.

The High Court dismissed the appellant's suit, reasoning that since the co-plaintiff was the rightful heir and had compromised, the defendant was now "clothed with the same rights" as the co-plaintiff.
law: A plaintiff who has a possessory title (i.e., was in possession of a property) is entitled to have that possession restored if they are dispossessed by a trespasser who has no right, title, or interest in the property.
A compromise entered into by one co-plaintiff does not extinguish the independent rights or claims of another co-plaintiff who is not a party to that compromise.
A co-plaintiff withdrawing from a suit via a compromise petition does not legally transfer their property rights to the defendant.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court was wrong to dismiss the appellant's suit solely because her co-plaintiff had compromised.

The Court emphasized that the appellant had her own independent claim based on her prior possession. Since the trial court found the defendant was a trespasser, the appellant was entitled to have her claim for restoration of possession decided on its own merits.

The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning that the defendant was "clothed with the rights" of the co-plaintiff. It questioned how a co-plaintiff could transfer her rights to a trespasser merely by filing a petition to withdraw from the suit.
The appellant's separate potential claim for a right to maintenance from the property also provided an independent basis for her suit to continue, irrespective of the co-plaintiff's actions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that it was an error to dismiss the appellant's suit. The compromise by a co-plaintiff could not defeat the appellant's independent right, based on her possessory title, to seek restoration of possession from a defendant who was found to be a mere trespasser.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a co-plaintiff could transfer all her rights to the defendant, who was a trespasser, by merely filing a petition stating she did not wish to prosecute the suit.
appellant_arguments: A co-plaintiff cannot transfer her rights to a defendant, found to be a mere trespasser, simply by filing a petition to withdraw from the suit, as this does not constitute a valid transfer of title.
respondent_arguments: The compromise and petition filed by the co-plaintiff (Jugli Bai) effectively transferred her rights as the rightful heir to the defendant, thereby clothing him with the same rights she possessed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a plaintiff's possessory title is sufficient evidence of title to obtain restoration of possession against a defendant who is a mere trespasser with no title.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was in possession of the properties before being dispossessed by the respondent, who was a trespasser. Therefore, her possessory title is sufficient to entitle her to restoration of possession from the trespasser.
respondent_arguments: The appellant's possessory title is irrelevant because the respondent is not a mere trespasser; he acquired the rights of the rightful heir (Jugli Bai) through a compromise, giving him a superior claim.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the appellant's suit on the ground that a co-plaintiff had entered into a compromise with the defendant.
appellant_arguments: The suit should not have been dismissed based on a compromise between a co-plaintiff and the defendant, as the appellant was not a party to that compromise and it could not affect her independent rights, such as her possessory title.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's dismissal was correct because the compromise was lawfully recorded and did not adversely affect the appellant, as she had no right, title, or interest in the suit lands to begin with.

cases.principle: Possession is sufficient evidence of title as owner against a defendant who has no title and is a mere wrong-doer. A person in possession can obtain a declaration of title and an injunction to restrain a wrong-doer from interfering with his possession.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Possession of property is sufficient evidence of title as owner against a person who has no title and is a mere wrongdoer. A person in possession is entitled to a declaration of title and an injunction to restrain a wrongdoer from interfering with that possession.
obiter: A widow may be entitled to remain in possession of property by virtue of her claim or right to maintenance until a proper arrangement for payment of maintenance is made by the person claiming the estate.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was in error in dismissing the appellant's suit based on a compromise entered into by her co-plaintiff, Jugli Bai. A co-plaintiff cannot transfer her rights to a defendant found to be a mere trespasser by merely filing a petition stating she does not wish to prosecute the suit. The appellant's possessory title is sufficient to entitle her to restoration of possession against the respondent, who, as a trespasser, had no right, title, or interest whatsoever.
legal_tests_applied: The possession of the plaintiff is sufficient evidence of title as owner against a defendant who has no title and is a mere wrong-doer.

If a person dispossessed otherwise than in due course of law can recover possession even from a person who might be able to prove a title (under s. 9 of the Specific Relief Act), it is certainly right and just that they should be able to obtain a declaration of title and an injunction against a person who has no title and is a mere wrong-doer.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court dismissed the appellant's suit because it erroneously considered that a compromise between the co-plaintiff (Jugli Bai) and the respondent justified the dismissal, a finding the Supreme Court reversed.
why_respondent_won: The High Court incorrectly reasoned that the respondent was 'clothed with the very same rights which were possessed by Jugli Bai' as a result of the compromise, a conclusion the Supreme Court found difficult to understand and ultimately rejected.
policy_considerations: It is right and just that a person in possession should be able, against a person who has no title and is a mere wrong-doer, to obtain a declaration of title as owner, and an injunction to restrain the wrong-doer from interfering with his possession.
